name: Abaloparatide

lead: Abaloparatide (Tymlos) is a prescription injectable that stimulates bone formation. Looksmaxxing forums discuss it alongside bonesmashing, puberty and limb lengthening, hoping for thicker facial bone and a stronger jaw and cheekbone structure.

It is a synthetic analogue of parathyroid hormone-related protein that activates the PTH1 receptor, increasing osteoblast activity and new bone formation. The phase 3 ACTIVE trial reported fewer new vertebral fractures versus placebo in postmenopausal women; no published study tests it for facial bone, height or appearance.

paras: Its approved use is as an injectable for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men at high fracture risk. Forum use is theoretical or anecdotal and is discussed as a complement to bone-focused or lengthening approaches.

The label lists osteosarcoma risk, low blood pressure on standing, high calcium and allergic reactions, and advises avoiding it with open growth plates. It is prescription-only and approved for osteoporosis, not for appearance.

angle.text: Abaloparatide is an approved osteoporosis drug that builds bone by activating the PTH1 receptor, and forum users speculate it could thicken facial bone for a stronger jaw and cheekbone structure. Trials have studied it for fracture risk in osteoporosis; none address facial bone or appearance.

lead: Abaloparatide (brand name Tymlos) is a synthetic 34-amino-acid analogue of parathyroid hormone-related protein, PTHrP(1-34), approved in the United States for osteoporosis. Its US label covers postmenopausal women at high fracture risk and men with osteoporosis at high risk, as an injectable bone-forming (anabolic) drug [1][2].

The pivotal phase 3 ACTIVE trial reported that abaloparatide reduced new vertebral fractures versus placebo in postmenopausal women [3]. Its approved use is for people with osteoporosis; it is not approved for height, skull, jaw or other appearance purposes.

On looksmax.org, abaloparatide and the related drug teriparatide are discussed in threads about bone density, bonesmashing, puberty and limb lengthening. These discussions are theoretical or anecdotal; no published study has tested it for those goals. The label carries warnings including osteosarcoma risk avoidance in patients with open epiphyses [2].
infobox: Subcutaneous injection (approved); a transdermal patch has been tested
Osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and men at high fracture risk [2]

paras: The US label indicates abaloparatide for treating postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk or who have failed or are intolerant to other therapy, and to increase bone density in men with osteoporosis under the same conditions [2]. Grokipedia reports FDA approval in April 2017 for women and an extension to men in December 2022, and a lifetime treatment limit of about two years owing to osteosarcoma findings in rodents [1].

No regulatory approval or published study supports appearance uses. Forum participants have proposed it as an adjunct to bonesmashing, as a possible aid to skeletal development during puberty and as a way to strengthen bone during limb lengthening [4][5][6].

According to the label, abaloparatide is an agonist at the PTH1 receptor, activating cAMP signalling and stimulating new bone formation on trabecular and cortical surfaces through osteoblast activity; in rats and monkeys it increased bone mineral density and strength [2]. A 2016 study described its selectivity for particular receptor conformations and the resulting downstream signalling [7]. Grokipedia and forum posts describe it as having more transient signalling and less resorption than PTH analogues, though the primary studies in the sources reviewed address receptor selectivity rather than this comparison [1][7].

In ACTIVE, a phase 3 double-blind randomised trial in postmenopausal women, abaloparatide 80 micrograms versus placebo was assessed for new vertebral fractures [3]; Grokipedia reports vertebral fracture rates of 0.6% versus 4.2% on placebo over 18 months [1]. An earlier phase 2 study reported effects on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women [8]. Network meta-analyses and reviews of osteoporosis drugs include abaloparatide among agents compared for fracture prevention [9][10][11].

Registered trials include a study in men with osteoporosis (ATOM) [12], a transdermal microneedle-patch phase 3 trial in postmenopausal women [13], a large real-world cardiovascular-safety study [14], and early-effect bone-tissue and surgical-setting studies [15][16]. All study populations are people with osteoporosis or healthy volunteers; no trial in adolescents, for height, or for cosmetic bone changes was found.

The label lists hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis, osteosarcoma risk (avoid in patients with open epiphyses and certain bone diseases), orthostatic hypotension, hypercalcaemia, and hypercalciuria or urolithiasis; the most common adverse reactions are hypercalciuria, dizziness, nausea, headache, palpitations, fatigue and upper abdominal pain [2]. The label states that it is not indicated for females of reproductive potential and that there are no human pregnancy data [2].

A looksmax.org thread proposes combining abaloparatide from informal sources with bonesmashing and orthodontics to build bone mass [4]. Another thread asks whether PTH analogues taken during puberty would have an effect, with replies saying the drugs are bone-anabolic [5]. A third proposes pairing it with limb lengthening to speed or strengthen bone formation [6]. Poster accounts describe obtaining it outside prescription channels; sourcing details are not reproduced here.

lore.intro: Looksmax.org threads discuss abaloparatide and teriparatide as bone-anabolic drugs that might support bonesmashing, skeletal development or limb lengthening [4][5][6].
